screens.title: Security Best Practices for Solana Programs
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contract vulnerabilities on Solana can produce permanent loss of funds or broken system invariants. In this chapter you will adopt a security-first mindset that begins at design time and continues through testing and audit. We will examine the most common pitfalls: reentrancy-like risks when performing cross-program invocations, signer spoofing, owner and type checks, arithmetic overflow and underflow, rigorous account validation for CPIs, rent and freeze authority concerns, and input validation. Each topic includes a concrete mitigation you can apply immediately, such as the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern, using require_signer! and require_owner_eq!, and switching to checked arithmetic APIs. You will also work through a hands-on lab: a deliberately vulnerable counter program which demonstrates missing owner and signer checks and an unsafe arithmetic operation. The lab asks you to add explicit ownership verification, require the correct signer, and replace raw arithmetic with checked operations. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain why each check matters, give a small code fix for each vulnerability, and outline a short audit checklist to reduce common errors. Consider what three security checks you would add first when designing a new token or marketplace program.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

First, you will learn to spot common issues such as missing owner checks, absent signer validation, and unsafe arithmetic; for each you will see the explicit code pattern that fixes the issue. Second, you will internalize defensive programming around CPIs by applying the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern so your program updates state before delegating to an untrusted callee. Third, you will learn how to validate account inputs thoroughly: check owner, type, writeability, and authority, and use the Pack trait when validating SPL Token accounts. Finally, you will build habits for safe arithmetic and error handling by using checked_add and returning clear program errors. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Lab Objectives
Lab step checklist
  • Confirm counter account owner equals program_id; return IllegalOwner otherwise.
  • Enforce user_signer.is_signer; return MissingRequiredSignature when absent.
  • Replace raw addition with checked_add and return an arithmetic error on overflow.
Why this order?

The order enforces authority and type safety before mutating state. Validations protect against spoofing and malicious inputs prior to any change.

Validation patterns

Use require_owner_eq! and require_signer! macros or explicit comparisons, and use custom error enums for clear diagnostics and testing.

Outcome

A hardened counter program that demonstrates ownership, signing, and safe arithmetic patterns you can reuse.

screens.title: Reentrancy-like Risks and Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI)
screens.narratorSegment: Reentrancy is commonly associated with multi-call EVM attacks, but on Solana a similar risk appears when your program performs a cross-program invocation to an untrusted callee and then modifies state afterwards. The core problem is trust: once you hand control to another program, that program can perform further instructions that affect shared accounts in the same transaction or later transactions. The recommended mitigation is the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. First perform all validation checks: confirm ownerships, signers, writeability, and input ranges. Second, apply all state changes and persist them. Third, perform external interactions such as CPIs. This order ensures that even if the callee attempts to call back into your logic, your state is already consistent and cannot be exploited by a later instruction. A concrete example is a token vault transfer that decrements a balance before invoking an untrusted swap; the decrement should persist so a malicious callee cannot observe an inconsistent state and cause double-spend. A common misconception is thinking Solana's single-threaded runtime removes all reentrancy risk; it reduces classic EVM-style reentry, but CPIs still create trust boundaries that must be respected. Key takeaway: always apply effects before interactions to limit the attack surface and preserve invariants.

keyIdea.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, update your program's state, then safely call other programs — never mutate state after calling an untrusted CPI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › CEI Pattern
Checks-Effects-Interactions
Process Flow
Checks
Validate ownership, signer presence, writeability and ranges for instruction data before any state change.
Effects
Apply state mutations and persist them so invariants hold even if a callee misbehaves.
Interactions
Make CPIs only after state is stable. Treat all callees as untrusted by default.
Concrete example
Imagine a vault program that transfers tokens via CPI. If you call the token program first and then update your vault balance, a malicious callee could cause inconsistent state or a double transfer. Instead, decrement the internal balance and serialize the account, then invoke the token transfer.
Common mistake
Believing Solana's single-threaded nature removes all reentrancy risk; CPIs still open a trust boundary.
Key Takeaway

Apply validation, persist state, then interact with external programs. That order prevents reentrancy-like exploits.

screens.title: Signer Spoofing and Authorization
screens.narratorSegment: The is_signer flag indicates that an account signed the transaction, but it alone does not prove that the signer is authorized to perform a particular action for your program. A common attack is to pass a signed account that is not the legitimate authority for the operation or to misuse PDAs without proper invoke_signed handling. To prevent signer spoofing, combine signer checks with explicit identity verification. Use require_signer! or check account. is_signer for critical accounts, and also verify the account key matches the expected authority key. For program-controlled PDAs, ensure the program derives the PDA with the correct seeds and calls invoke_signed when a signed PDA is required. A concrete example: an admin-only configuration update should check that the provided signer key equals the admin public key and that is_signer is true. A typical misconception is treating is_signer as synonymous with authorization: it only verifies that the account produced a signature for the transaction. Key practice: require both presence of the signature and validation that the signer is the expected authority, or use PDAs with invoke_signed when the program must sign on behalf of a PDA.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Signer Spoofing
Problem
is_signer shows the account signed the transaction, but it does not confirm that the signer has the authority you expect. An attacker could sign with their own key and attempt operations reserved for another role if your code only checks is_signer.
Mitigation
  • Check account.is_signer and also confirm account.key equals the expected authority.
  • For PDAs, derive the PDA locally and use invoke_signed to sign CPIs.
Concrete example
Admin update: require signer and verify accounts[0].key == &admin_key. If using a PDA admin, use invoke_signed with the correct seeds.
Common mistakes
  • Relying on is_signer alone for authorization checks.
  • Assuming a PDA will be treated as signed without invoking invoke_signed.
Key Takeaway

Combine signer checks with identity verification; use PDAs and invoke_signed correctly when your program must sign.

screens.title: Owner Checks and Type Spoofing
screens.narratorSegment: Assuming an account is a particular type without checking its owner is risky. A malicious user can pass an account with arbitrary data that your program will deserialize and misinterpret. The primary defense is explicit owner verification: check account. owner == &EXPECTED_PROGRAM_ID before deserializing or using the account. For SPL Token accounts verify owner == &spl_token::ID so you do not treat arbitrary data as a token account. For your program-owned state accounts, verify owner == program_id. When deserializing more complex data, include a magic number, version, or enum discriminant so you can validate the intended type after deserialization. A concrete example: before calling Pack::unpack on an SPL Token account, confirm the owner equals the SPL Token program ID and that the account data length matches expected token account size. A common misconception is trusting that a passed account is the right type because its public key looks familiar; keys and data are separate. Key practice: always combine owner checks with type-confirming fields and fail loudly when mismatches are detected. Owner Checks and Type Spoofing means explicitly check account.owner and confirm type markers to avoid type spoofing and mis-deserialization.. In practical terms, verify account.owner and confirm expected data types before deserializing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Owner & Type Checks
Owner check checklist
  • Confirm account.owner == &EXPECTED_PROGRAM_ID before deserialization.
  • For SPL Token accounts, check owner == &spl_token::ID and use Pack to validate structure.
  • Include a magic number or enum variant in your state to confirm type after deserialization.
Concrete example
If you expect a token account, check owner equals spl_token::ID and that the data parses successfully via Pack::unpack; otherwise reject the instruction.
Common mistake
Deserializing arbitrary account data without owner checks can lead your program to treat attacker-controlled bytes as valid structured state.
Watch out

Always fail fast on owner mismatch; use require_owner_eq! or explicit comparison to return a clear error.

screens.title: Arithmetic Overflow and Checked Arithmetic
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic bugs are among the most serious and easiest to exploit. In debug builds, Rust arithmetic panics on overflow, but in release builds arithmetic may wrap silently, producing incorrect results such as negative balances or unexpectedly large numbers. On Solana programs, values like token amounts commonly use u64 or u128, and an unchecked add or subtract can let an attacker manipulate amounts to drain funds. The mitigation is to use checked arithmetic primitives: checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul, and checked_div. These functions return an Option that you must convert into an error when None is returned. For example, replace current_balance + amount with current_balance. checked_add(amount). ok_or(ProgramError::ArithmeticOverflow)? or with a custom error. A practical misconception is assuming tests will catch overflow; tests often use small numbers and won't expose boundary cases. Always treat arithmetic as a security boundary and perform explicit checks with clear error paths. This small change prevents wraparound exploits and improves the clarity of your program's error handling. Arithmetic Overflow and Checked Arithmetic means use checked arithmetic and return explicit errors to prevent silent wraparound in release builds.. In practical terms, use checked_add / checked_sub to avoid wraparound bugs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use checked arithmetic and return explicit errors to prevent silent wraparound in release builds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Checked Arithmetic
Why checked arithmetic

Unchecked math can wrap in release builds and produce incorrect balances. Checked functions return None on overflow so you can fail safely.

// BAD: can overflow silently
let new_balance = current_balance + amount;

// GOOD: handles overflow gracefully
let new_balance = current_balance.checked_add(amount)
  .ok_or(ProgramError::ArithmeticOverflow)?;
Practical tips
  • Convert Option to a clear ProgramError or a custom error enum so tests can assert failures.
  • Validate input ranges to reduce likelihood of edge-case overflows.
  • Use u128 for aggregations but still apply checked arithmetic.
Key Takeaway

Replace raw operators with checked_* APIs and convert None to explicit errors to avoid silent wraparound.

screens.title: CPI Authorization and Account Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-program invocations delegate authority and trust to another program. Because you pass accounts to the callee, you must rigorously validate each account's properties before invoking. That validation should include: owner verification, is_writable for accounts expected to be mutated, is_signer when a signature is required for the callee's logic, and any structure or mint checks for token accounts. For example, when invoking the SPL Token Program to transfer tokens, ensure source and destination accounts are owned by spl_token::ID, that they refer to the same mint, and that the authority you pass is the legitimate owner or delegate. A failure to validate any of these could let an attacker substitute malicious accounts or cause the callee to panic and abort the transaction. Practical validation steps: use Pack::unpack or Pack::unpack_unchecked to confirm token account layout after owner check, confirm writeable flags for accounts the callee needs to modify, and include explicit authority checks. A common misconception is trusting the callee to perform these checks for you. Treat the callee as untrusted: validate everything you pass to it. CPI Authorization and Account Validation means before a cpi, confirm owner, writeability, signer flags, and structural validity such as token mints and sizes.. In practical terms, validate every account you pass to a callee. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › CPI Validation
CPI pre-flight checklist
Pre-validate
  • Ownership: account.owner == expected program ID.
  • Writeability: accounts that will be mutated must be writable.
  • Signer: ensure the authority is a proper signer or a correctly derived PDA with invoke_signed.
  • Structure: use Pack to deserialize SPL token accounts and confirm mint matches.
Concrete risk

If you pass an attacker-controlled account as a destination, they can receive funds meant for another recipient. If you pass an invalid type, the callee may panic and cause denial of service.

Pro Tip

Validate ownership and structure before calling the callee; log clear messages to ease audits and tests.

screens.title: Rent Exemption and Freeze Authority
screens.narratorSegment: Account lifecycle matters for long-lived program state and vaults. Accounts that are not rent-exempt can be reclaimed and closed by the network when their balance drops below the required minimum, which may lead to unexpected loss of program-owned state. When creating program-owned accounts intended to remain, ensure they hold enough SOL to remain rent-exempt. For SPL Token accounts, freeze_authority gives a party the power to freeze transfers; if a vault has an undesirable freeze_authority, tokens can be locked unexpectedly. Consider setting freeze_authority to None or to a trusted multisig when creating token accounts used as vaults. A common mistake is ignoring these meta-properties when designing systems that expect permanence. Validate rent exemption status where appropriate and minimize privileged authorities; prefer multisig or remove freeze authority for critical vaults. These steps reduce administrative attack surface and keep state stable across program upgrades and runtime conditions. Rent Exemption and Freeze Authority means ensure program-owned accounts are rent-exempt and set freeze authorities intentionally to avoid accidental or malicious locking of tokens.. In practical terms, protect critical accounts from closure and freezing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Account permanence matters
keyIdea.text: Ensure program-owned accounts are rent-exempt and set freeze authorities intentionally to avoid accidental or malicious locking of tokens.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Rent & Freeze
Rent exemption

Accounts that are not rent-exempt can be reclaimed and closed. For program-owned storage, allocate sufficient SOL to remain rent-exempt to avoid accidental closure.

Practical measure
When creating accounts, calculate rent exemption and fund accordingly. Verify rent exemption status where account permanence is required.
Freeze authority

SPL Token accounts can be frozen by a freeze authority. Vaults should avoid giving freeze authority to a single key; prefer None or a multisig to prevent unexpected freezes.

Key Takeaway

Plan account funding and authority settings at creation time to prevent administrative or network-level failures later.

screens.title: Input Validation: Never Trust User Data
screens.narratorSegment: User-supplied instruction data and account lists must be validated against your program's business rules. Never assume correct lengths, ranges, or public key formats. Input validation should include range checks for token amounts, length checks for strings or arrays, and format checks for public keys. If you expect an account list of a fixed size or particular order, enforce it and return a clear error when the layout is incorrect. For example, check that an amount is non-zero and within an allowed maximum before applying arithmetic or transfers, and assert that public keys match expected authorities. A subtle misconception is assuming the client or UI enforces constraints; on-chain validation is the ultimate authority. Use custom errors to make it clear which validation failed so tests can assert expected error conditions. Input validation reduces the chance of logical errors, panics, and exploitable edge cases. screens.title: Vulnerable Counter Walkthrough — Identify Flaws
screens.narratorSegment: Now we apply the patterns to a concrete example: a deliberately vulnerable counter program. The supplied code reads a counter account and a user signer, increments the value, logs it, and serializes the data. The explicit issues are: missing owner check for the counter account, missing signer check for the user_signer, and an unchecked addition that risks overflow. Walk through the code and mark where each check should occur. First, before deserializing the counter account, verify counter_account. owner equals the program_id and return IllegalOwner if not. Second, confirm that user_signer. is_signer is true and return MissingRequiredSignature otherwise. Third, replace the raw increment with checked_add and return an ArithmeticOverflow error if it fails. Consider adding a small custom error enum so each failure maps to an interpretable error during tests. pub struct CounterAccount { pub value: u32 }

// ... inside process_instruction
let counter_account = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
let user_signer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;

let mut counter_data = CounterAccount::try_from_slice(&counter_account.data.borrow())?;

// VULNERABILITY: unchecked arithmetic

counter_data.serialize(&mut &mut counter_account.data.borrow_mut()[..])?;

  • Checked arithmetic: counter_data.value = counter_data.value.checked_add(1).ok_or(CounterError::ArithmeticOverflow)?;

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Counter Fixes
Fixed snippet
// Custom error enum placeholder
// enum CounterError { IllegalOwner, MissingRequiredSignature, ArithmeticOverflow }

// Owner check
if counter_account.owner != program_id {
  msg!("Counter account is not owned by this program.");
  return Err(CounterError::IllegalOwner.into());
}

// Signer check
if !user_signer.is_signer {
  msg!("User must be a signer to increment the counter.");
  return Err(CounterError::MissingRequiredSignature.into());
}

// Checked arithmetic
counter_data.value = counter_data.value
  .checked_add(1)
  .ok_or(CounterError::ArithmeticOverflow.into())?;

counter_data.serialize(&mut &mut counter_account.data.borrow_mut()[..])?;
Testing guidance
  • Negative tests: pass wrong owner and assert IllegalOwner is returned.
  • Signature tests: call without signer and assert MissingRequiredSignature.
  • Overflow test: set value to max and ensure ArithmeticOverflow is raised.
Key Takeaway

Applying these edits and testing failure modes prevents the main classes of exploit demonstrated by the vulnerable counter.

fullNarratorScript:
Smart contract vulnerabilities on Solana can produce permanent loss of funds or broken system invariants. In this chapter you will adopt a security-first mindset that begins at design time and continues through testing and audit. We will examine the most common pitfalls: reentrancy-like risks when performing cross-program invocations, signer spoofing, owner and type checks, arithmetic overflow and underflow, rigorous account validation for CPIs, rent and freeze authority concerns, and input validation. Each topic includes a concrete mitigation you can apply immediately, such as the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern, using require_signer! and require_owner_eq!, and switching to checked arithmetic APIs. You will also work through a hands-on lab: a deliberately vulnerable counter program which demonstrates missing owner and signer checks and an unsafe arithmetic operation. The lab asks you to add explicit ownership verification, require the correct signer, and replace raw arithmetic with checked operations. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain why each check matters, give a small code fix for each vulnerability, and outline a short audit checklist to reduce common errors. Consider what three security checks you would add first when designing a new token or marketplace program.

In this chapter you will practice identifying real vulnerabilities and implementing practical defenses. First, you will learn to spot common issues such as missing owner checks, absent signer validation, and unsafe arithmetic; for each you will see the explicit code pattern that fixes the issue. Second, you will internalize defensive programming around CPIs by applying the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern so your program updates state before delegating to an untrusted callee. Third, you will learn how to validate account inputs thoroughly: check owner, type, writeability, and authority, and use the Pack trait when validating SPL Token accounts. Finally, you will build habits for safe arithmetic and error handling by using checked_add and returning clear program errors. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify your skill with a small hands-on lab and checklist.

This lesson pairs conceptual checks with a lab where you edit a counter program to harden it. You will practice three concrete fixes: enforce that the counter account is owned by your program, require the incrementing user to be a signer, and replace unchecked addition with checked_add. Beyond that lab, you will practice validating accounts before each CPI, checking is_writable and ownership for each passed account, and using the Pack trait to confirm SPL Token accounts. You will also review rent exemption and freeze authority risks. Performing these tasks in sequence trains you to reason about trust boundaries: what you control directly, what you verify, and what you must treat as untrusted. This objective ensures you not only know the patterns, but can apply them in code and tests to confidently reduce common attack surfaces.

Reentrancy is commonly associated with multi-call EVM attacks, but on Solana a similar risk appears when your program performs a cross-program invocation to an untrusted callee and then modifies state afterwards. The core problem is trust: once you hand control to another program, that program can perform further instructions that affect shared accounts in the same transaction or later transactions. The recommended mitigation is the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. First perform all validation checks: confirm ownerships, signers, writeability, and input ranges. Second, apply all state changes and persist them. Third, perform external interactions such as CPIs. This order ensures that even if the callee attempts to call back into your logic, your state is already consistent and cannot be exploited by a later instruction. A concrete example is a token vault transfer that decrements a balance before invoking an untrusted swap; the decrement should persist so a malicious callee cannot observe an inconsistent state and cause double-spend. A common misconception is thinking Solana's single-threaded runtime removes all reentrancy risk; it reduces classic EVM-style reentry, but CPIs still create trust boundaries that must be respected. Key takeaway: always apply effects before interactions to limit the attack surface and preserve invariants.

The is_signer flag indicates that an account signed the transaction, but it alone does not prove that the signer is authorized to perform a particular action for your program. A common attack is to pass a signed account that is not the legitimate authority for the operation or to misuse PDAs without proper invoke_signed handling. To prevent signer spoofing, combine signer checks with explicit identity verification. Use require_signer! or check account. is_signer for critical accounts, and also verify the account key matches the expected authority key. For program-controlled PDAs, ensure the program derives the PDA with the correct seeds and calls invoke_signed when a signed PDA is required. A concrete example: an admin-only configuration update should check that the provided signer key equals the admin public key and that is_signer is true. A typical misconception is treating is_signer as synonymous with authorization: it only verifies that the account produced a signature for the transaction. Key practice: require both presence of the signature and validation that the signer is the expected authority, or use PDAs with invoke_signed when the program must sign on behalf of a PDA.

Assuming an account is a particular type without checking its owner is risky. A malicious user can pass an account with arbitrary data that your program will deserialize and misinterpret. The primary defense is explicit owner verification: check account. owner == &EXPECTED_PROGRAM_ID before deserializing or using the account. For SPL Token accounts verify owner == &spl_token::ID so you do not treat arbitrary data as a token account. For your program-owned state accounts, verify owner == program_id. When deserializing more complex data, include a magic number, version, or enum discriminant so you can validate the intended type after deserialization. A concrete example: before calling Pack::unpack on an SPL Token account, confirm the owner equals the SPL Token program ID and that the account data length matches expected token account size. A common misconception is trusting that a passed account is the right type because its public key looks familiar; keys and data are separate. Key practice: always combine owner checks with type-confirming fields and fail loudly when mismatches are detected. Owner Checks and Type Spoofing means explicitly check account.owner and confirm type markers to avoid type spoofing and mis-deserialization.. In practical terms, verify account.owner and confirm expected data types before deserializing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Arithmetic bugs are among the most serious and easiest to exploit. In debug builds, Rust arithmetic panics on overflow, but in release builds arithmetic may wrap silently, producing incorrect results such as negative balances or unexpectedly large numbers. On Solana programs, values like token amounts commonly use u64 or u128, and an unchecked add or subtract can let an attacker manipulate amounts to drain funds. The mitigation is to use checked arithmetic primitives: checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul, and checked_div. These functions return an Option that you must convert into an error when None is returned. For example, replace current_balance + amount with current_balance. checked_add(amount). ok_or(ProgramError::ArithmeticOverflow)? or with a custom error. A practical misconception is assuming tests will catch overflow; tests often use small numbers and won't expose boundary cases. Always treat arithmetic as a security boundary and perform explicit checks with clear error paths. This small change prevents wraparound exploits and improves the clarity of your program's error handling. Arithmetic Overflow and Checked Arithmetic means use checked arithmetic and return explicit errors to prevent silent wraparound in release builds.. In practical terms, use checked_add / checked_sub to avoid wraparound bugs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cross-program invocations delegate authority and trust to another program. Because you pass accounts to the callee, you must rigorously validate each account's properties before invoking. That validation should include: owner verification, is_writable for accounts expected to be mutated, is_signer when a signature is required for the callee's logic, and any structure or mint checks for token accounts. For example, when invoking the SPL Token Program to transfer tokens, ensure source and destination accounts are owned by spl_token::ID, that they refer to the same mint, and that the authority you pass is the legitimate owner or delegate. A failure to validate any of these could let an attacker substitute malicious accounts or cause the callee to panic and abort the transaction. Practical validation steps: use Pack::unpack or Pack::unpack_unchecked to confirm token account layout after owner check, confirm writeable flags for accounts the callee needs to modify, and include explicit authority checks. A common misconception is trusting the callee to perform these checks for you. Treat the callee as untrusted: validate everything you pass to it. CPI Authorization and Account Validation means before a cpi, confirm owner, writeability, signer flags, and structural validity such as token mints and sizes.. In practical terms, validate every account you pass to a callee. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Account lifecycle matters for long-lived program state and vaults. Accounts that are not rent-exempt can be reclaimed and closed by the network when their balance drops below the required minimum, which may lead to unexpected loss of program-owned state. When creating program-owned accounts intended to remain, ensure they hold enough SOL to remain rent-exempt. For SPL Token accounts, freeze_authority gives a party the power to freeze transfers; if a vault has an undesirable freeze_authority, tokens can be locked unexpectedly. Consider setting freeze_authority to None or to a trusted multisig when creating token accounts used as vaults. A common mistake is ignoring these meta-properties when designing systems that expect permanence. Validate rent exemption status where appropriate and minimize privileged authorities; prefer multisig or remove freeze authority for critical vaults. These steps reduce administrative attack surface and keep state stable across program upgrades and runtime conditions. In practical terms, protect critical accounts from closure and freezing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Input validation should include range checks for token amounts, length checks for strings or arrays, and format checks for public keys. If you expect an account list of a fixed size or particular order, enforce it and return a clear error when the layout is incorrect. Security is a continuous process. During audits and code reviews apply a short, repeatable checklist for every instruction handler. First, confirm authority: verify owners and signers and validate PDAs and invoke_signed usage. Second, validate inputs: ranges, lengths, and public key expectations. Third, ensure arithmetic uses checked_* operations and custom errors for failures. Fourth, pre-validate all accounts that will be passed to CPIs: owners, writeability, mint matches, and authority. Fifth, apply CEI ordering so state mutates before interactions. Sixth, verify account permanence properties like rent-exemption and freeze authority. Seventh, write negative tests that exercise each failure mode: wrong owner, missing signer, overflow case, and malformed accounts. Eighth, prefer clear, small functions with single responsibility so logic is easy to audit. These three cards summarize the most essential concepts. First, reentrancy-like risk: even though Solana is single-threaded, CPIs create trust boundaries so you must update state before calling external programs. Second, signer and owner checks: is_signer only indicates a signature was included; always verify that the signer or owner matches the expected key or program ID and use PDAs with invoke_signed when appropriate. Third, arithmetic safety: use checked_add, checked_sub, and friends and return explicit errors when they fail. Keep these three checks in every handler: authority, validated inputs, and safe arithmetic. When you combine them with thorough CPI validation and CEI ordering, most common exploits are preventable.
